lessonTitle: Standards and the Safety Case: Hazards, Guarding and Lockout

blocks.text: A student team builds a small press for crushing aluminium cans. It works, the demonstration goes well, and then the supervisor asks one question: 'What stops a hand being inside when it closes?' There is no guard, no emergency stop and no way to isolate the hydraulic pressure for maintenance. Safety is not a feature added at the end; it is a set of requirements, taken from standards and from a hazard assessment, that shapes the design from the start.

blocks.markdown: **Standards** are documents agreed by technical experts that describe accepted ways to design, test and document a product. Some are made mandatory by regulation, others are voluntary but represent the accepted state of the art, which a court or a customer may expect you to have followed. A **safety case** is the structured argument, with evidence, that a product is acceptably safe: what hazards exist, how each is controlled and why the remaining risk is acceptable.

blocks.title: Choosing applicable standards
blocks.text: The standards that apply depend on three things: **what the product is** (a machine, a pressure vessel, an electrical appliance, a lifting device), **where it will be sold or used** (the legal framework of the market, such as machinery regulations), and **which hazards it presents** (moving parts, electrical energy, noise, pressure, heat). For a machine in a typical European or international setting examples include a general principles standard for machinery risk assessment (ISO 12100), a standard on design of guards (ISO 14120), one on emergency stop (ISO 13850) and one on electrical equipment of machines (IEC 60204-1). These are examples; always check the current edition and its applicability.

blocks.markdown: **Hazard assessment.** The method is: (1) identify hazards across the life of the machine (installation, use, cleaning, maintenance, fault, foreseeable misuse); (2) estimate the risk of each as the combination of **severity** $S$ of the harm and the **likelihood** $L$ of it occurring, each on an agreed scale; (3) rank the hazards; (4) apply controls; (5) re-estimate the risk after controls (the *residual risk*) and judge whether it is acceptable.

blocks.caption: Risk score from a severity rating S and a likelihood rating L, each on a 1-5 scale (illustrative). The product ranks hazards but is not a measure of probability. Safety-critical severities need separate attention.

rows: Redesign so that the crushing zone cannot be reached by a hand
Substitute a less hazardous material or process, for example a lower-pressure hydraulic fluid or a lower-force electric drive
Guard or interlock that works without the operator's cooperation
Protective equipment worn by the operator
blocks.caption: Hierarchy of risk controls, from most to least effective.

blocks.title: Ranking and re-scoring hazards
blocks.prompt: For the can crusher the team rates: crushing of a hand (S = 4, L = 4); hydraulic hose burst (S = 3, L = 3); noise during use (S = 2, L = 5). Compute the risks, rank them, and re-score the crushing hazard after adding an interlocked guard that reduces the likelihood to 1.

steps.text: Risk before controls: multiply severity by likelihood for each hazard.
Ranking: crushing (16), noise (10), hose burst (9). Crushing is addressed first.
Re-score with the interlocked guard: severity is unchanged because a failure would still cause serious harm, but likelihood falls to 1.

blocks.answer: Crushing risk falls from 16 to 4 (a 75% reduction); severity is unchanged, so the hazard still receives attention.

blocks.markdown: **Guarding, emergency stop and lockout.** A **fixed guard** prevents access to a hazard and can be removed only with tools. An **interlocked guard** stops the hazardous motion when the guard is opened, and the machine must not restart merely because the guard is closed. The guard must be positioned so that the hazard has stopped before a hand reaches it. A simple estimate, in the form used by ISO 13855, is: distance $\ge$ approach speed $K$ $\times$ (response time + stopping time), plus an intrusion allowance $C$. A commonly used approach speed is $K=1600$ mm/s, and ISO 13855 gives 2000 mm/s for distances up to 500 mm (check the current edition). An **emergency stop** is a clearly marked, easily reached, latching control that brings the machine to a safe state, and resetting it must not by itself restart the machine; it is a complementary measure, not a substitute for guarding. **Lockout** (with tagging) is the procedure for maintenance: stop the machine, isolate every energy source (electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity or spring), lock each isolator with the lock of the person working, release or block stored energy, and verify that the machine cannot start (a 'try' test).

blocks.caption: Minimum distance from the guard opening to the hazard (m): K is the approach speed (m/s), t_response + t_stop is the total time from opening the guard to the hazard coming to rest (s), C is the intrusion allowance for reaching through openings (m). Values are taken from the applicable standard for real designs; here they are assumed.

blocks.title: Position of an interlocked guard
blocks.prompt: An interlock detects guard opening and the press stops, in total, after 0.25 s (response time plus stopping time). Assume an approach speed K = 1.6 m/s and no intrusion allowance (C = 0). What is the minimum distance from the opening to the hazard? Would it be acceptable at 0.30 m?

steps.text: Distance covered by the hand while the press stops.
Compare: $0.30<0.40$ m, so a hand could reach the hazard before it stops.
Remedies: move the guard opening further away, reduce the stopping time (a faster brake), or reduce the stroke speed.

blocks.answer: The minimum distance is 0.40 m, so 0.30 m is not acceptable.

items: Identify the standards that apply from product type, market and hazards, and say why.
List hazards for every phase of use and rate severity and likelihood.
Apply controls in the order of the hierarchy and re-rate the residual risk.
Specify guards, emergency stop and isolation points on the drawings.
Record the argument and evidence in the safety case.

blocks.title: Controls must not rely on good behaviour
blocks.text: A control that works only if the operator remembers it (a warning sign) ranks below one that works regardless (a fixed guard). When a guard can be bypassed easily, people will bypass it.

blocks.title: Standards are not a substitute for judgement
blocks.text: Compliance with a standard shows a recognised level of care, but the hazard assessment must still cover the specific machine. Standards are revised, so state the edition used.

points: Applicable standards follow from the product type, the market and the hazards, and the reason for each is recorded.
Hazards are rated by $S\times L$ before and after controls, using the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineer, inform, protect.
Guards must be placed so the hazard stops before a hand arrives; emergency stop and lockout complete the machine's safety measures.

questions.stem: A team designs a conveyor that will be sold to customers in several countries. Which approach correctly identifies the standards that apply?

options.text: Identify the product type, the markets and legal framework, and the hazards, then select standards covering each and note the reason
Use whichever standard the team already owns
Use no standards because a prototype is not a product
Apply only the standard for paint finish

questions.correctOptionText: Identify the product type, the markets and legal framework, and the hazards, then select standards covering each and note the reason

distractorRationale.a: Correct: applicability follows product, market and hazards.
distractorRationale.b: Ownership of a standard is not a reason for applicability.
distractorRationale.c: A product intended for sale must meet the applicable requirements.
distractorRationale.d: Paint is not the main hazard of a conveyor.

questions.explanation: Standards are selected by what the product is, where it will be used and which hazards it presents. Recording the reason makes the selection reviewable.

questions.stem: A reviewer asks why a team cites a recognised guard-design standard. Which answer is most appropriate?

options.text: It describes an accepted way to design guards for the hazard, and following it is evidence that the safety requirement is met
It avoids having to do a hazard assessment
It guarantees that no accident can ever happen
It replaces the need for an emergency stop

questions.correctOptionText: It describes an accepted way to design guards for the hazard, and following it is evidence that the safety requirement is met

distractorRationale.a: Correct: standards represent accepted practice and provide evidence of due care.
distractorRationale.b: The hazard assessment is still needed.
distractorRationale.c: No standard can guarantee zero risk.
distractorRationale.d: An emergency stop is a separate measure.

questions.explanation: A relevant standard describes accepted practice, which supports the safety case. It does not remove the duty to assess hazards specific to the product.

questions.stem: According to the hierarchy of risk controls, which action should be considered first?

options.text: Eliminate the hazard by design
Give operators personal protective equipment
Add a warning label
Provide training

distractorRationale.a: Correct: removing the hazard is the most effective control.
distractorRationale.c: Labels depend on people reading and following them.

questions.explanation: The hierarchy ranks controls by reliability. Eliminating the hazard works regardless of human behaviour, while information and PPE depend on it.

questions.stem: On a rotary cutting machine, which of the following is an engineering control?

options.text: A fixed guard that covers the rotating blade
A sign reading 'Keep hands clear'
A training session on safe working
Safety gloves

questions.correctOptionText: A fixed guard that covers the rotating blade

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a guard works without relying on the operator.

questions.explanation: Engineering controls physically separate people from the hazard. Signs, training and gloves all depend on operator action and sit lower in the hierarchy.

questions.stem: What is the correct principle for isolating a machine for maintenance (lockout)?

options.text: Stop it, isolate all energy sources, lock and tag the isolators, release stored energy, then verify that it cannot start
Switch it off at the control panel and put up a note
Isolate the electricity only, since hydraulics are harmless when switched off
Remove the lock when the first person leaves the machine

questions.correctOptionText: Stop it, isolate all energy sources, lock and tag the isolators, release stored energy, then verify that it cannot start

distractorRationale.a: Correct: all energy sources, locking, and verification are needed.
distractorRationale.b: A panel switch can be reset by someone else and does not remove stored energy.
distractorRationale.c: Hydraulic and gravity energy can still cause movement.
distractorRationale.d: Each worker keeps their own lock until they have finished.

questions.explanation: Lockout means every energy source is isolated, held isolated by a personal lock, and proved isolated by trying to start. Stored energy is released or blocked.

questions.stem: A hazard is rated severity 4 and likelihood 3 on 1 to 5 scales. Compute the risk score, using risk $=S\times L$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The score is $4\times3=12$. The number only has meaning when compared with other hazards rated on the same scales.

questions.stem: A hazard has an initial risk score of 20 (severity 4, likelihood 5). A control reduces the likelihood to 2 and leaves severity unchanged. By what percentage does the risk score fall?
questions.explanation: The new score is $4\times2=8$, and $(20-8)/20=0.60$, or 60%. Severity is unchanged, so the hazard still needs to be reviewed.

questions.stem: An interlocked guard stops a machine 0.45 s after the guard is opened. Assume an approach speed K = 1.6 m/s and an intrusion allowance C = 0.10 m for reaching through the opening. Using $S\ge K(t_{\mathrm{response}}+t_{\mathrm{stop}})+C$ with the total time given, find the minimum distance from the guard opening to the hazard in metres.
questions.explanation: The hand travels $K\times(t_{\mathrm{response}}+t_{\mathrm{stop}})=1.6\times0.45=0.72$ m while the machine stops. Adding the allowance gives $0.72+0.10=0.82$ m.

questions.stem: A school workshop will use a small benchtop CNC mill built by a student team. State which categories of standard should be considered, say why each applies, and explain what additional information you would need.
markingGuide: Machinery safety general principles and risk assessment, because the product is a machine with hazards
Guarding and interlocks, because of rotating cutter and moving axes
Emergency stop requirements for a machine that can cause injury
Electrical safety of equipment, because of mains supply and motor drives
Mentions noise, dust and coolant where relevant
Need market and jurisdiction, user type (children) and intended use to refine the list
questions.explanation: Applicability is derived from the product type, the hazards and the user environment. A school setting raises the level of guarding required because of the inexperience of the users.

questions.stem: A pallet-wrapping machine has a rotating turntable with a pinch point under its edge, a hydraulic lift and a mains motor. Perform a hazard assessment of two hazards with S and L before controls, propose controls from the hierarchy, give residual ratings, and describe the lockout steps for maintenance and the role of an emergency stop.
markingGuide: Two hazards identified (for example pinch under turntable, hydraulic energy release) with S and L and calculated risks
Controls in the order of the hierarchy (eliminate or guard first, then information, PPE)
Residual ratings re-computed and justified (for example likelihood reduced, severity retained)
Lockout steps: stop, isolate electrical and hydraulic energy, lock and tag, release stored hydraulic or gravity energy, verify
Emergency stop: easily reached, latching, no automatic restart on reset, complementary to guarding
Mentions interlocked guard and stopping distance consideration
questions.explanation: A good assessment gives numerical ratings before and after controls and shows that severity may remain high even when likelihood falls. Lockout covers all energy sources, and the emergency stop supplements rather than replaces guarding.
